newsitem.title: UK: Dlr/mark at 6-yr peak in Europe, stg tops 3 marks.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/mark at 6-yr peak in Europe, stg tops 3 marks.

text.p: The dollar and sterling continued their relentless climb on Friday to their highest levels since 1991 as traders ignored Bundesbank warnings about excessive mark weakness and pummeled the German unit across the board.
Dealers said there was no fresh news behind the latest dollar surge and technical trading took over.
Sterling/mark traded above 3.00 marks for the first time since April 1991 and the psychological magnet of such a round number was key to the day's trading.
Traders said there was no sign of either Bundesbank or Bank of England intervention despite recent vocal concerns.

"If the Bundesbank does nothing to stop a sustained move in dollar/mark above these levels, we could see the mark falling significantly everywhere - a move that would be totally inconsistent with their public calls for stable exchange rates," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago in London.

The mark gleaned only fleeting support Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer on Thursday, when he said the correction of dollar/mark from 1995 lows was over and the Bundesbank was interested in a strong mark moving into European monetary union.
Yet traders merely used the slightly higher mark levels today as more attractive rates at which to sell.
Continual rumours of Bundesbank orders for marks permeated the market late Thursday and early Friday but traders could not confirm any dealings and dismissed talk of intervention.
At 1530 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.7705/10 marks, up two pfennigs from 1.7505/10 late Thursday and and just off its new high at 1.7732 set earlier. Its 1994 peak was 1.7686.

Sterling/mark rose as high as 3.0010, its highest since October 1990, in tandem with dollar/mark's rise. Mark/lira, mark/yen and mark/French franc all reversed modest gains made Thursday and skidded lower aswell. The mark's trade weighted index is at its lowest since 1994, analysts said.

"The driving force behind today's move was the attraction of these key levels on sterling and the dollar, with the round figure on sterling/mark providing the main focus," said Stuart Frost, market analyst at NatWest Markets.

The mark spiral lower over the past year has been fostered by relatively low German interest rates, consistently high levels of unemployment there and the prospect of the mark'S replacement in 18 months time with a single European currency.
Concerns the new euro will now include traditionally less stable currencies like the Italian lira has accelerated mark selling while hopes of a punctual EMU start remain buoyant.
The dollar and sterling, meantime, have relatively high interest rate returns and UK interest rates at least are expected to rise further next month.
A more benign inflationary performance in the U.S., seen again today in news of a 0.1 percent drop in U.S. producer prices in June, has clouded the rate out there slightly.

For sterling, however, a perceived lack of fiscal tigthening in last week's UK budget has led to market players to bet on a steeper rise in interest rates from the newly independent Bank of England in order to stem consumer demand.
Key UK rates rose a 1/4-point on Thursday to 6.75 percent.
Sterling's surge has caused problems for the Irish punt within Europe's exchange rate mechansim (ERM), meantime.
The punt has been dragged higher by sterling's surge as the Irish economy is booming in tandem with the UK business cycle and because of a high degree of trade between the two countries.

The punt, however, has risen as much as 13 percent above its ERM parity against the weakest ERM unit, the French franc and is only allowed to deviate 15 percent under ERM rules. There was speculation today the Bank of France sold punts for francs to stabilise the situation, traders said.
--Mike Dolan, London newsroom +44 171 542 6762
